title: Singly linked list: insertion, input & recursion
overview: This module turns the hand-built list into real operations: insert at the head, at the tail (slow and O(1) versions), and at any index, plus reading a list from input until `-1`. It explains why `head` must be passed as a reference to a pointer, and uses recursion to print a list backwards. The practice day applies these to size, duplicates, the middle element, indexed inserts and a sorted check.

concepts.explain: Passing `Node* head` gives the function a copy of the address, so changing `head` inside does nothing outside. `Node* &head` passes the pointer itself, so the caller sees the new head.
Point the new node at the current head, then make the new node the head. Order matters: link first, move head second.

concepts.term: Insert at tail, O(n) vs O(1)
concepts.explain: Without a tail pointer you walk to the last node every time (O(n)). Keeping a `tail` pointer lets you attach directly and move `tail` forward (O(1)).
When `head == NULL` there is no node to attach to, so the new node becomes both head and tail.
Walk to the node just before the position (`idx - 1` steps), then point the new node at its successor and the previous node at the new node.
Read values in a loop and stop when you see `-1`; each other value is added at the tail.
Call the function on `next` first and print afterwards. The prints then happen while the calls return, from the last node back to the first.
When values are small (at most 100), a `bool visited[101]` array detects repeats in one pass.

files.title: Passing a pointer by reference
files.what: Compares `fun(int* p)`, which gets a copy of the pointer, with `fun2(int* &p)`, which gets the caller's pointer itself.
steps: In `main`, `p` points to `x = 10`.
`fun(p)` prints `*p` (10), then makes its own copy point to a local `y`. `main`'s `p` is untouched, so `*p` is still 10.
`fun` prints `&p`, the address of its copy, which differs from `main`'s `&p`.
`fun2(p)` sets `p = NULL`. Because `p` is a reference, `main`'s pointer really becomes NULL.
`fun2` prints the same address as `main`'s `&p`, showing it is the same variable.
files.output_note: Addresses vary per machine. Compare them: inside `fun` the address of `p` differs from `main`'s, while inside `fun2` it equals `main`'s. The `10` line shows `fun` did not change `main`'s pointer.
files.watch_out: After `fun2`, `p` is NULL, so `*p` would crash. Also, pointing a pointer at a local variable (`p = &y`) that outlives the function would leave it dangling.

check.q: Why does `insert_at_head` need `Node* &head` rather than `Node* head`?
check.a: It changes which node `head` points to; without the reference, only the function's copy would change.

files.title: Insert at head
files.what: Adds new nodes in front of the list in O(1).
steps: `insert_at_head` creates `newNode`, sets `newNode->next = head`, then `head = newNode`.
Insert 100, 200, 300; each becomes the new first node.
Print the list.
files.output_note: `300 200 100 10 20 30`, one per line. The last value inserted is first.
files.watch_out: Swapping the two lines (`head = newNode` first) makes the new node point to itself and loses the old list.

check.q: Inserting 1, 2, 3 at the head of an empty list gives what order?

files.title: Insert at head (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of `insert_at_head.cpp`. The only difference is that `print_linked_list` takes `Node* &head`, which is unnecessary but harmless because it does not change `head`.
steps: Same list, same three head inserts, same print.

check.q: Does a print function need the head by reference?
check.a: No. It only reads the list, so a plain `Node*` copy is enough.

files.title: Insert at tail (walk to the end)
files.what: Appends nodes by walking from `head` to the last node each time.
steps: If `head == NULL`, the new node becomes `head`.
Otherwise move `tmp` until `tmp->next == NULL` (the last node).
Set `tmp->next = newNode`.
Append 100, 200, 300 to `10 -> 20 -> 30` and print.
files.output_note: `10 20 30 100 200 300`, one per line: new values appear in the order they were added.
files.watch_out: Building a list of n values this way costs O(n^2) in total.

check.q: Why does the walk stop at `tmp->next == NULL` here instead of `tmp == NULL`?
check.a: We need to stand on the last node to attach to it; `tmp == NULL` would walk past it.

files.title: Insert at tail (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of `insert_at_tail.cpp`, but the constructor has a bug that makes it run forever.
steps: Same list and same three tail inserts as the original.
files.output_note: No useful output: the program times out while walking to the tail.
files.watch_out: The constructor says `this->next = next;` which copies the uninitialised member into itself, so `next` holds garbage instead of NULL. The walk to the tail follows garbage addresses and never ends. Fix: `this->next = NULL;`.

check.q: Why must the constructor set `next = NULL`?
check.a: Every loop over the list stops on NULL; a garbage `next` makes loops run into random memory.

files.title: Insert at tail in O(1) with a tail pointer
files.what: Keeps a `tail` pointer to the last node so appending needs no walk.
steps: Build `10 -> 20 -> 30` and let `tail` point to the 30 node.
`insert_at_tail(head, tail, val)` takes both pointers by reference.
Empty list: `head = tail = newNode`.
Otherwise `tail->next = newNode` and `tail = newNode`.
Append 100, 200, 300 and print.
files.output_note: Same result as the slow version: `10 20 30 100 200 300`. Only the speed differs.
files.watch_out: The `tail` pointer must always be kept in sync. If another function adds or removes the last node, it must update `tail` too.

check.q: Why is `tail` passed by reference?
check.a: The function moves `tail` to the new node, and the caller must see that change.

files.title: Insert at tail O(1) (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of the optimized tail insert, with the function renamed `insert_at_tail_optimized`. It does not compile.
steps: Same idea: attach at `tail`, then move `tail`.
files.output_note: No output: compile error.
files.watch_out: `a->next = b;` uses `b`, which does not exist here (the third node is called `tail`). Write `a->next = tail;`. The constructor also has `this->next = next;`, which must be `this->next = NULL;`.

check.q: In this program, which node should `a->next` point to?
check.a: The node stored in `tail` (value 30).

files.title: Insert at any index
files.what: Inserts a value at a 0-based position in the middle of the list by walking to the node just before it.
steps: Start with `10 -> 20 -> 30`.
`insert_at_any_index` moves `tmp` from head `idx - 1` times (the loop starts at `i = 1`), landing on the node before position `idx`.
`newNode->next = tmp->next` keeps the rest of the list attached.
`tmp->next = newNode` links the new node in.
Insert 1000 at index 2, then 2000 at index 2, then 3000 at index 3.
files.complexity: Time O(idx) per insert · Space O(1)
files.output_note: `10 20 2000 3000 1000 30`. Trace it: after the first insert `10 20 1000 30`; 2000 goes in front of 1000; 3000 goes between 2000 and 1000.
files.watch_out: There is no check for index 0 (use insert at head) or for an index past the end (`tmp` would become NULL and crash).

check.q: What happens if you swap the two linking lines?
check.a: `tmp->next` is overwritten first, so `newNode->next` points to `newNode` itself and the rest of the list is lost.

files.title: Insert at any index (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of `insert_at_any_index.cpp` with the same three inserts, but with the constructor bug `this->next = next;`.
steps: Same inserts as the original; the two linking statements are written on one line.
files.complexity: Time O(idx) per insert · Space O(1)
files.output_note: The first six lines are correct (`10 20 2000 3000 1000 30`). Then random numbers repeat forever until the program times out.
files.watch_out: The last node's `next` is garbage instead of NULL, so printing runs past the end into random memory. Fix the constructor to `this->next = NULL;`.

check.q: Why do the first six values still print correctly?
check.a: Those nodes' `next` pointers were set explicitly by the program; only the last node keeps the garbage `next`.

files.title: Read a linked list until -1
files.what: Starts with an empty list and adds each input value at the tail (O(1) with a tail pointer) until `-1` appears.
steps: `head` and `tail` start as NULL.
Loop: read `val`; stop on `-1`.
Otherwise call `insert_at_tail(head, tail, val)`.
Print the list.
files.input_note: Values separated by spaces, ending with -1.
files.output_note: `10 20 30 40`, one per line, in input order. The `-1` is not stored.
files.watch_out: If the input ends without `-1`, `cin >> val` fails, `val` keeps its last value and the loop never ends. `while (cin >> val && val != -1)` is safer.

check.q: Why does the first insert need a special case?
check.a: With an empty list there is no tail node to attach to, so the new node becomes both head and tail.

files.title: Read a linked list (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of `input_a_linked_list.cpp` with no real changes.
steps: Same reading loop and O(1) tail insert.
files.output_note: Same output: `10 20 30 40`.

check.q: What would the list look like if you used insert at head instead?
check.a: Reversed: 40 30 20 10.

files.title: Recursion: print forward and backward
files.what: Two recursive functions: print-then-recurse gives 1..5, recurse-then-print gives 5..1. This is the idea behind printing a list in reverse.
steps: Base case: stop when `i > n`.
`recursion_1_to_n` prints `i` before calling itself with `i+1`, so numbers come out on the way down.
`recursion_n_to_1` calls itself first and prints afterwards, so numbers come out on the way back up.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) call stack
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4 5` then `5 4 3 2 1`, one per line.

check.q: Which print happens first in `recursion_n_to_1(1, 5)`?
check.a: 5, printed by the deepest call once `i = 6` returns.

files.title: Print a linked list in reverse
files.what: Reads a list and prints it backwards with recursion, without changing any links.
steps: Read values until `-1` and append each at the tail.
`print_reverse(tmp)` returns immediately if `tmp` is NULL.
Otherwise it first calls `print_reverse(tmp->next)`.
Only after that call returns does it print `tmp->val`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) call stack
files.output_note: `40 30 20 10`, one per line: the reverse of the input order.
files.watch_out: Very long lists (hundreds of thousands of nodes) can overflow the call stack.

check.q: Does `print_reverse` change the list?
check.a: No. It only reads nodes; the list stays 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40.

files.title: Print in reverse (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of `reverse_linked_list_printing.cpp` with a typo that stops it compiling.
steps: Same reading loop and recursive reverse print.
files.output_note: No output: compile error.
files.watch_out: `cout << tmp->val << end;` should be `endl`. With that fix it prints `40 30 20 10`.

check.q: What is the base case of `print_reverse`?
check.a: `tmp == NULL`: return without printing.

files.title: Size of a linked list
files.what: Reads a list and counts its nodes with `get_size`.
steps: Build the list from input until `-1`.
`get_size` walks from head and adds 1 for each node until NULL.
Print the count.
files.output_note: `7`: seven values before the `-1`.

check.q: What does `get_size` return for an empty list?
check.a: 0: the loop never runs because `head` is NULL.

files.title: Size of a linked list (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of the size program with no real changes.
steps: Same build and count.
files.output_note: `4`: duplicates count as separate nodes.

check.q: How could you track the size in O(1) instead of walking the list?
check.a: Keep a counter and increase it on every insert (and decrease it on every delete).

files.title: Does the list have a duplicate?
files.what: Uses a `visited` array of 101 booleans (values are at most 100) to spot a repeated value in one pass.
steps: Build the list.
Walk it; if `visited[tmp->val]` is already true, print `YES` and return.
Otherwise mark `visited[tmp->val] = true` and move on.
If the walk finishes, print `NO`.
files.output_note: `YES`: the second 4 is found already marked.
files.watch_out: The array only works because values are at most 100. A value above 100 would write outside the array.

check.q: Why size the array 101 and not 100?
check.a: Value 100 needs index 100, which exists only when the size is 101.

files.title: Has duplicate (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy, except `has_duplicate` is declared `bool` while still printing and using a bare `return;`.
steps: Same visited-array logic.
files.output_note: `YES`, same as the original.
files.watch_out: A `bool` function must return a value. It only compiles here because of the `-fpermissive` flag; a normal compiler rejects `return;`. Either make it `void` or return `true`/`false` and print in `main`.

check.q: How would you rewrite it to return a bool properly?
check.a: Return `true` when a repeat is found and `false` at the end; `main` prints YES or NO based on the result.

files.title: Print the middle element(s)
files.what: Finds the size first, then walks to the middle. For an even size it prints both middle values.
steps: Build the list and compute `size` with `get_size`.
Even size: walk `size/2 - 1` steps and print `tmp->val` and `tmp->next->val`.
Odd size: walk `size/2` steps and print `tmp->val`.
files.output_note: First line `6` is the size (a debug print), then `3 4`, the two middle values of an even-length list.
files.watch_out: The extra `cout << size` line would fail a judge that expects only the middle values; remove it. An empty list would crash on `tmp->val`.

check.q: For `2 4 6 8 10`, how many steps does `tmp` take and what is printed?
check.a: 2 steps (size/2), printing 6.

files.title: Insert at index with queries
files.what: Intended to read a list, then for each `(index, value)` query insert at head, tail or middle (or print Invalid) and print the list. As written it never finishes.
steps: Read the list until `-1` (intended).
For each query, get the current `size`.
Index below 0 or above `size`: print `Invalid`.
Index 0: insert at head. Index equal to `size`: insert at tail. Otherwise insert in the middle.
Print the list (intended after every query).
files.complexity: Time O(n) per query · Space O(n)
files.input_note: List values ending with -1, then lines of `index value`.
files.output_note: No output: the program runs until the time limit.
files.watch_out: The first loop never reads input (`cin >> val` is missing), so it checks an uninitialised `val` and inserts forever. Fix: `while (cin >> val && val != -1)`. Also, the list is printed only once at the end (it should print after each valid query), each value goes on its own line, and on an empty list index 0 would insert twice (both `idx == 0` and `idx == size` match); use `else if`.

check.q: Which index values are valid for a list of size 3?
check.a: 0, 1, 2 and 3 (0 = head, 3 = tail).

files.title: Is the list sorted ascending?
files.what: Despite the file name, this checks whether the list is in ascending order by comparing each node with the next one.
steps: Read values with `while (cin >> val)` and stop on `-1`.
`ascending_sort_check` looks at each node `tmp` and its `tmp->next`.
If the next value is smaller, print `NO` and return.
If the walk finishes, print `YES`.
files.input_note: Values ending with -1. This input breaks the order at the very first pair, the only kind of input the buggy loop can finish on.
files.output_note: `NO`, because 2 is smaller than 5.
files.watch_out: The loop never moves `tmp` forward (`tmp = tmp->next;` is missing), so whenever the first pair is in order it loops forever. Add `tmp = tmp->next;` at the end of the loop body. An empty list would also crash on `tmp->next`.

check.q: After fixing the bug, what does `1 5 6 8 9 -1` print?
check.a: YES.

recap: Pass `head` (and `tail`) as `Node* &` whenever the function may change them.
Head insert: `newNode->next = head; head = newNode;`, O(1).
Tail insert is O(1) with a tail pointer, O(n) without.
Middle insert: stop one node early, link the new node to the rest first, then link the previous node to it.
Always set `next = NULL` in the constructor; garbage pointers cause endless loops.
Recurse first, print later to print a list backwards.

check_yourself.q: What is wrong with `void insert_at_head(Node* head, int val)`?
check_yourself.a: The function changes only its copy of `head`, so the caller's list never gets the new first node.

check_yourself.q: Why is building a list of n values with the walking tail insert O(n^2)?
check_yourself.a: Each insert walks the whole current list: 1 + 2 + ... + n steps in total.

check_yourself.q: To insert at 0-based index 3, which node must `tmp` stop on?
check_yourself.a: The node at index 2, the one just before the new position.

check_yourself.q: How much extra memory does recursive reverse printing use?
check_yourself.a: O(n), one stack frame per node.
